articles.title: O que é abandono de trabalho? Entenda o caso de Eduardo Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-deputado foi demitido por abandono de cargo após processo disciplinar; veja o que diz a legislação e quais são as diferenças entre servidores públicos e trabalhadores da iniciativa privada.
articles.summary: Caso de Eduardo Bolsonaro reacende dúvidas sobre abandono de cargo e as diferenças entre as regras para servidores públicos e trabalhadores da iniciativa privada.
articles.body:
O Ministério da Justiça oficializou, nesta segunda-feira (21), a demissão do ex-deputado federal Eduardo Bolsonaro do cargo de escrivão da Polícia Federal (PF) .

A demissão ocorreu por infração disciplinar de “abandono de cargo”, após a apuração de que Eduardo teria faltado ao serviço, sem justificativa, por mais de 30 dias consecutivos .

A decisão foi assinada pelo ministro Wellington Lima e Silva na última sexta-feira (18) e publicada no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) desta segunda.

A saída encerra o vínculo de Eduardo com uma carreira que tem remuneração inicial superior a R$ 14 mil e permite progressão salarial ao longo dos anos de serviço.

Embora a expressão "abandono de trabalho" seja relativamente conhecida, muita gente ainda tem dúvidas sobre o que ela significa na prática.

🤔 Afinal, faltar 30 dias consecutivos leva automaticamente à demissão? Existe um prazo definido em lei? E o que muda quando o trabalhador atua no setor público em vez da iniciativa privada?

As respostas variam de acordo com o regime de contratação. Enquanto trabalhadores com carteira assinada são regidos pela Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT) e pela jurisprudência da Justiça do Trabalho, servidores públicos estão submetidos a estatutos próprios e a procedimentos administrativos específicos.

Ou seja, as regras para apurar a conduta e as consequências para o trabalhador são diferentes.

Veja as principais diferenças na tabela abaixo.

Apesar das diferenças entre os regimes, um ponto costuma gerar confusão: a ideia de que existe um prazo que transforma automaticamente uma ausência em abandono de trabalho. Na prática, não é tão simples.

A CLT prevê o abandono de emprego como hipótese de justa causa, mas não estabelece quantos dias de ausência são necessários para caracterizá-lo.

Ao longo dos anos, os tribunais passaram a adotar o período de 30 dias como referência para analisar os casos, mas não como uma regra automática, explica Gustavo Fonseca Monteiro, advogado trabalhista empresarial e sócio da Tahech Advogados.

Segundo ele, a Justiça costuma exigir dois elementos: ausência prolongada e injustificada e intenção do empregado de não retornar ao trabalho.

"Faltar ao trabalho por um período e abandonar o emprego não são a mesma coisa (...) para que exista abandono, as circunstâncias devem demonstrar que o empregado não pretende retornar e decidiu, ainda que sem uma comunicação formal, romper o vínculo" .

🔎 Essa intenção é conhecida no meio jurídico como "animus abandonandi". Em outras palavras, não basta que o trabalhador esteja ausente. É preciso haver indícios de que ele decidiu, de fato, encerrar a relação de emprego.

Felipe Mazza, coordenador da área de Direito Trabalhista do Efcan Advogados, explica que os 30 dias funcionam apenas como um parâmetro.

"A empresa deve avaliar as circunstâncias concretas e buscar demonstrar que o empregado decidiu romper, por sua conduta, a continuidade da relação de trabalho".

Por isso, uma pessoa pode ficar mais de um mês sem trabalhar e, ainda assim, não ter abandonado o emprego. Uma internação, uma doença grave, problemas relacionados a benefícios previdenciários ou dificuldades relevantes de comunicação podem afastar essa conclusão.

Para que a justa causa seja aplicada, é necessário demonstrar algo além da ausência: a intenção de não retornar ao trabalho.

Esse cuidado existe porque situações excepcionais são comuns, pontua Taunai Moreira, sócio do escritório Bruno Boris Advogados.

Um trabalhador pode não conseguir avisar a empresa imediatamente porque está hospitalizado, enfrenta uma doença grave ou outro impedimento relevante, exemplifica.

O que a empresa precisa fazer antes de demitir?

Se a intenção do trabalhador é um dos elementos centrais da análise, cabe à empresa reunir provas antes de aplicar a demissão por justa causa.

O procedimento normalmente começa pela verificação de eventuais justificativas para as faltas, como:

Internações ou licenças devem ser consideradas antes de qualquer decisão.

Na sequência, recomenda-se tentar contato pelos meios habituais, como telefone, e-mail e aplicativos de mensagens, registrando todas as tentativas realizadas.

Caso o trabalhador permaneça sem responder, a empresa deve formalizar uma convocação para que retorne ao trabalho ou apresente justificativas.

Monteiro explica que o documento deve informar o período de ausência, convocar o trabalhador a retornar ou apresentar justificativa em prazo razoável e advertir expressamente que a falta de manifestação poderá caracterizar abandono de emprego e resultar em demissão por justa causa.

"A convocação deve ser enviada por meio que permita comprovar tanto o seu conteúdo quanto a entrega, como por exemplo carta registrada com aviso de recebimento ou, conforme o caso, notificação extrajudicial. E-mail e mensagens também podem reforçar a prova, desde que seja possível demonstrar o envio e o recebimento".

Embora a legislação não determine um número mínimo de notificações, os especialistas recomendam que todas as tentativas sejam documentadas. Isso pode fazer diferença caso a situação seja discutida posteriormente na Justiça do Trabalho.

"Sem isso, a justa causa não se sustenta", afirma Taunai, lembrando que o ônus da prova recai sobre o empregador.

O que o trabalhador perde se houver abandono?

Eduardo Bolsonaro, ex-deputado federal e filho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro — Foto: Bruno Spada/Câmara dos Deputados

Quando a demissão por abandono é confirmada, os efeitos são os mesmos de uma dispensa por justa causa.

Nesse caso, o empregado deixa de receber:

saque imediato do FGTS em razão da rescisão;

férias proporcionais acrescidas de um terço.

Por outro lado, alguns direitos permanecem preservados. A empresa continua obrigada a pagar o saldo de salário referente aos dias efetivamente trabalhados e as férias já adquiridas, mas ainda não usufruídas.

Outra dúvida comum envolve o FGTS. O dinheiro depositado na conta vinculada não é perdido e continua pertencendo ao trabalhador, embora ele não possa sacá-lo imediatamente em razão daquela demissão.

Se, nas empresas privadas, a caracterização do abandono costuma ser discutida posteriormente na Justiça do Trabalho, na administração pública a apuração precisa ocorrer antes de qualquer punição.

Para os servidores federais submetidos à Lei nº 8.112, o abandono de cargo é definido como ausência intencional por mais de 30 dias consecutivos.

🔎 No caso dos policiais federais, uma legislação específica prevê a demissão por 30 dias consecutivos de faltas injustificadas ou 60 dias alternados em um período de 12 meses.

Mesmo quando a legislação estabelece critérios objetivos, porém, a punição não é automática.

"A Administração não pode aplicar a demissão imediatamente: deve instaurar um Processo Administrativo Disciplinar", explica Felipe Mazza.

Segundo Monteiro, o PAD é indispensável para que a administração pública identifique o período de ausência, avalie possíveis justificativas e assegure ao servidor o direito de apresentar provas e se defender.

"A perda do cargo é uma sanção grave e está sujeita ao devido processo legal, ao contraditório e à ampla defesa", afirma.

Por isso, a conclusão de uma comissão disciplinar não significa necessariamente o encerramento do caso. Em situações como a de Eduardo Bolsonaro, a comissão apenas recomenda a penalidade, e a decisão final cabe à autoridade competente.

O que aconteceu no caso de Eduardo Bolsonaro?

Eduardo Bolsonaro mora nos Estados Unidos desde o início de 2025. Na época, afirmou que deixou o Brasil por se considerar alvo de perseguição política.

Em dezembro daquele ano, a Mesa Diretora da Câmara dos Deputados decretou a perda do mandato por excesso de faltas. Com isso, ele deixou de ter o afastamento que permitia exercer a atividade parlamentar sem atuar na Polícia Federal .

A PF, então, determinou que ele retornasse ao cargo de escrivão. Segundo a corporação, porém, Eduardo Bolsonaro não se reapresentou.

Diante da ausência, a Corregedoria da Polícia Federal abriu, em janeiro de 2026, um Processo Administrativo Disciplinar para apurar um possível abandono de cargo. Após concluir a investigação, a PF recomendou a demissão do ex-deputado e encaminhou o processo ao Ministério da Justiça.

Como a corporação é subordinada ao ministério, caberá ao ministro Wellington Lima e Silva decidir se aplica ou não a penalidade.

articles.title: Partido de Putin conquista número recorde de assentos no Parlamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Sigla Rússia Unida conquistou 355 das 450 cadeiras na Duma, a câmara baixa do Parlamento russo, em pleito com oposição vetada. Kremlin celebrou resultado e falou em 'coesão' em torno do presidente, já o bloco europeu chamou eleição de 'erosão da democracia'.
articles.summary: Sigla Rússia Unida conquistou 355 das 450 cadeiras na Duma, a câmara baixa do Parlamento russo, em pleito com oposição vetada. Kremlin celebrou resultado e falou em 'coesão' em torno do presidente, já o bloco europeu chamou eleição de 'erosão da democracia'.
articles.body:
O partido Rússia Unida, do presidente Vladimir Putin , conquistou um número recorde de 355 cadeiras na Duma, a câmara baixa do Parlamento russo, que tem 450 assentos, segundo resultados preliminares divulgados nesta segunda-feira (21) pela chefe da comissão eleitoral, Ella Pamfilova.

Com quase todos os votos apurados após a eleição de três dias, da qual não participaram partidos críticos a Putin, os resultados mostraram que o partido presidencial terá uma supermaioria superior ao recorde anterior, registrado em 2016.

Essa eleição era tratada pelo Kremlin como particularmente importante, porque foi a primeira a ser realizada após o início da guerra da Ucrânia . O pleito serviria a Putin e sua equipe para medir o apoio do público russo ao conflito, que está em seu 5º ano sem perspectiva de ser finalizado.

Assim como o restante do aparato estatal russo, o Duma é subordinado ao governo Putin e as eleições parlamentares foram rigorosamente controladas e sem a participação de forças políticas contrárias à guerra na Ucrânia.

Presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin, durante discurso em 18 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Sputnik/Alexander Kazakov/Pool via REUTERS

O Kremlin celebrou nesta segunda o resultado da eleição e afirmou que a vitória esmagadora do partido de Putin mostra que os russos apoiam o presidente.

“Esses indicadores apontam, é claro, para o mais alto nível de coesão da sociedade russa em torno do chefe de Estado”, declarou o porta-voz do Kremlin, Dmitri Peskov, durante uma entrevista coletiva.

A Comissão Europeia afirmou que as eleições parlamentares russas mostraram uma “erosão contínua e crescente da democracia” e uma “repressão sistemática e institucionalizada” do governo Putin contra a oposição.

“As supostas eleições para a Duma representaram mais um grande retrocesso para a democracia russa. Seu resultado nunca esteve em dúvida. O Kremlin silenciou a dissidência, impediu a participação do único partido registrado que se opunha à sua guerra na Ucrânia e excluiu observadores eleitorais internacionais. O verniz de democracia é tudo o que resta na Rússia”, afirmou a alta representante da UE para a política externa, Kaja Kallas.

A oposição russa afirmou que a votação ficou longe de ser justa.

articles.title: Idoso desaparecido no Amazonas é encontrado após dois dias na mata | G1
articles.standfirst: Armando Azedo Ribeiro foi localizado por volta das 8h30 de domingo (21) em uma casa abandonada, a cerca de 12 quilômetros da residência, na comunidade São Sebastião do Jará.
articles.summary: Armando Azedo Ribeiro, idoso desaparecido no Amazonas, foi localizado em uma casa abandonada em Parintins após dois dias de buscas intensas na mata.
articles.body:
Idoso de 68 anos é encontrado após passar dois dias desaparecido em área de mata no interior do AM — Foto: Divulgação/CBMAM

Armando Azedo Ribeiro, de 68 anos, sobreviveu por dois dias perdido em uma área de mata na zona rural de Parintins , no interior do Amazonas. Ele foi encontrado na manhã de domingo (20), em uma casa abandonada, a cerca de 12 quilômetros de onde mora , depois de passar o período se alimentando de coco e bebendo água de um igarapé .

O idoso havia saído de casa na manhã de sexta-feira (18) para buscar frutas em uma plantação e não retornou .

Armando foi localizado por volta das 8h30, na comunidade São Sebastião do Jará. Segundo os bombeiros, ele estava consciente e comunicativo.

O idoso contou que ultrapassou uma área que conhecia e não conseguiu encontrar o caminho de volta.

As buscas foram realizadas por militares do 19º Grupamento de Bombeiros Militar (19º GBM) de Parintins, com apoio de moradores da comunidade.

A equipe chegou ao local por via fluvial e percorreu trilhas e áreas de mata próximas à residência e às plantações. O perímetro de buscas foi ampliado até que o idoso fosse encontrado.

Durante a operação, os bombeiros usaram equipamentos de comunicação, GPS e sinalização sonora.

Após o resgate, Armando foi entregue aos familiares.

articles.title: Hopi Hari: mãe de jovem que perdeu movimentos diz que ajuda parou | G1
articles.standfirst: Mãe de Júlia Bossoni revela que parque pagou apenas hospedagem e traslado enquanto família precisou custear R$ 70 mil em assistência médica.
articles.summary: A família de Júlia Bossoni, ferida na montanha-russa Montezum do Hopi Hari, afirma que o parque suspendeu a assistência médica e financeira após a alta hospitalar.
articles.body:
A família de Júlia Bossoni, de 21 anos, que sofreu traumatismo cranioencefálico e perdeu movimentos após andar na motanha-russa Montezum , no Hopi Hari, afirma que o parque deixou de prestar assistência à jovem após a alta hospitalar.

Em entrevista à EPTV , afiliada da TV Globo, a mãe Danielle Rimolli afirmou nesta segunda-feira (21) que o suporte financeiro do parque limitou-se ao período de internação inicial de 57 dias em Vinhedo (SP) e foi cortado logo após o retorno da jovem a Londrina (PR) .

Ela entrou na Justiça com processos cível e criminal contra o parque de diversões. A ação conjunta soma mais de 800 páginas e detalha o histórico médico da jovem. O caso, investigado pelo Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP), foi exibido pelo Fantástico deste domingo (20).

"Eles acionaram o seguro exclusivamente para pagar nossa hospedagem e alimentação por dois meses em Vinhedo. Para a Júlia, não foi feito absolutamente nada [...] Eles sumiram e não deram mais um centavo", afirma Danielle.

O g1 pediu uma posição ao Hopi Hari sobre a queixa da família. Nesta reportagem, veja a nota enviada pelo parque ao Fantástico.

A Montezum é a maior montanha-russa de madeira da América Latina . Inaugurada em 1999, cerca de de 42 metros de altura e pode alcançar uma velocidade de até 103 km/h em pouco mais de um quilômetro de extensão.

Segundo a mãe, representantes do parque prometeram enviar ajuda financeira semanal para custear fraldas, remédios e cadeira de rodas, mas deixaram de responder à advogada da família. O único valor pago após a alta em Vinhedo foi de R$ 7 mil, referente ao transporte de ambulância até o Paraná .

Para garantir o tratamento da jovem com uma equipe de neurocirurgiões especialistas, que não atendem pelo plano de saúde, a família precisou pagar R$ 70 mil do próprio bolso . O valor foi arrecadado por meio de uma vaquinha.

Jovem perde movimentos após andar em montanha-russa do Hopi Hari; MP investiga — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Paralelamente à disputa financeira, o quadro de saúde de Júlia apresentou regressão. A jovem precisou ser internada novamente entre 4 de agosto e 5 de setembro para passar por novas cirurgias na cabeça devido a complicações .

Durante o procedimento para recolocação da calota craniana, os médicos descobriram que o couro cabeludo da jovem havia colado diretamente no cérebro, afirma Danielli. A complicação decorreu da gravidade da primeira cirurgia de emergência, feita em abril.

O procedimento cirúrgico, estimado em uma hora e meia, durou mais de cinco horas para descolar a membrana sem causar novos danos. Após apresentar acúmulo de líquido na cabeça (hidrocefalia), Júlia passou por outros procedimentos.

"Ela não está como estava antes dessas cirurgias. Regrediu. Os movimentos, a fala e as reações ficaram bem limitados. Ela fala muito baixinho e se comunica pouco", relata Danielle. A rotina da jovem agora inclui sessões diárias de fisioterapia, fonoaudiologia e eletromodulação.

Jovem perde movimentos após andar em montanha-russa do Hopi Hari; MP investiga — Foto: Fantástico

Júlia não foi a primeira a sofrer um trauma ao andar na Montezum. Em 2018, aconteceu também com Nathalia Assenjo Motta. "Conforme a montanha-russa desceu e subiu para fazer a curva, o meu pescoço fez o mecanismo de chicote, deu aquele estalo. Meu corpo desligou totalmente.", relembra.

O deslocamento das vértebras foi tão grave que ela precisou colocar 12 pinos e duas hastes na região cervical. Três dias depois, a professora recuperou os movimentos do corpo, mas perdeu a mobilidade do pescoço. O Hopi Hari pagou uma indenização a Nathalia por danos materiais.

Hoje, ela ainda lida com uma rotina difícil. "Fisioterapias, hidroterapia que eu tive que pagar particular, que o plano não cobre. Eu tenho essas dores absurdas e preciso tomar remédios fortíssimos".

Márcio também foi vítima da Montezum, em 2014. Depois de andar na montanha-russa, ele ficou tetraplégico. O motoboy morreu em 2023, por complicações decorrentes de uma infecção urinária.

"Houve de fato o rompimento de duas vértebras, mas o problema neurológico que desenvolveu a tetraplegia, conforme consta do laudo, foi o movimento de chicote", diz o advogado João Erhardt.

Em uma plataforma de avaliação de consumidores, foram encontrados ao menos 40 registros feitos, nos últimos dois anos, por pessoas que alegam ter sofrido lesões ao andar na Montezum . Os relatos são de dores no pescoço, lesões no joelho e até costelas quebradas.

"A Montezum Possui certificação internacional emitida pelo Grupo TUV Nord, uma das maiores organizações de inspeção e testes de atrações do mundo. As inspeções acontecem anualmente no caso de atrações radicais como a Montezum, e bianuais, em atrações de baixa complexidade. Outros importantes protocolos de segurança, treinamento de pessoal e de atenção ao visitante fazem parte da rotina diária do Hopi Hari em todas as suas atrações. O parque também segue rigorosamente a norma nacional para parques de diversões 'ABNT NBR 15926-2023 Equipamentos de Parques de Diversão'.

Antes mesmo de acessar a Montezum, placas contendo dados sobre a atração estão colocadas em pontos de fácil visualização para que todos os visitantes tenham informações claras e detalhadas sobre o funcionamento da montanha russa, além de recomendações e restrições. Ainda quando estão na fila para acessar a atração, um sistema de áudio destaca as recomendações e restrições. E, no momento do embarque, os operadores da atração também reforçam as informações, por meio de um sistema de som. Os procedimentos seguem normas internacionais adotadas em atrações ao redor do mundo e integram rotinas obrigatórias de segurança e operação. De janeiro de 2026 até o momento, mais de 870 mil pessoas frequentaram o parque e, deste total, aproximadamente 470 mil pessoas passaram pela atração, que é a mais visitada do Hopi Hari.

Também é importante destacar que, recentemente, o Ministério Público emitiu parecer sobre a atração enfatizando não haver risco coletivo, defeito no projeto da montanha russa ou qualquer negligência. No texto do parecer, o MP destaca "a regularidade do funcionamento da atração "Montezum" sob a ótica da tutela coletiva e difusa da segurança e saúde dos consumidores". O parecer acrescenta, ainda, que "o estabelecimento prestador do serviço adota protocolos rigorosos de prevenção, manutenção e segurança operacional".

E enfatiza que 'a montanha-russa Montezum é submetida a rotinas periódicas de inspeção técnica diária , abrangendo a estrutura de madeira, trilhos, fixações, travas de segurança, cintos, sensores fotoelétricos, painéis elétricos e sistemas de frenagem, com supervisão por equipe de engenharia e certificações técnicas pertinentes. Ademais, constata-se a existência de sinalização visual e sonora no local, informando previamente a classificação da atração como radical, as forças e movimentos nela envolvidos, além das expressas contra indicações de uso a pessoas com problemas na coluna, gestantes e portadores de condições clínicas específicas', descreve o parecer. As placas indicativas com as informações nelas contidas, também estão anexadas neste email.

O Hopi Hari esclarece ainda que a visitante do Paraná acessou a atração por duas vezes no mesmo dia de sua visita ao parque, conforme imagens anexadas. A primeira ida à Montezum ocorreu às 11h da manhã e a segunda, cerca de cinco horas depois, por volta de 16h30 do mesmo dia.

O episódio envolvendo a jovem paranaense ocorreu em sua segunda passagem pela atração, quando apresentou um quadro de convulsão e recebeu pronto atendimento das equipes do parque, seguindo todos os protocolos de segurança. A providência inicial foi prestar os primeiros socorros no ambulatório do parque. A visitante foi encaminhada para a Santa Casa de Vinhedo, onde permaneceu internada até apresentar condições de retorno à sua cidade. A direção do parque acompanhou de perto o tratamento prestado, sempre em contato com os familiares, custeando as despesas durante a permanência em Vinhedo.

Vale ressaltar que o departamento jurídico do Hopi Hari também manteve contato com os familiares da visitante paranaense para o suporte necessário durante todo o processo de atendimento da paciente em seu tratamento. O corpo jurídico, assim como a direção do parque, seguem à disposição da família da visitante. Importante destacar também que o Hopi Hari dispõe de um seguro que foi franqueado à família.

O Hopi Hari segue investindo em normas, procedimentos e treinamentos visando a segurança das atrações do parque que, nos últimos 5 anos, já recebeu mais de 5,5 milhões de visitantes.

Sobre as ocorrências mencionadas de anos anteriores, esclarecemos que os dados pertencem a gestões passadas. A atual administração tem seu foco estrito na rigorosa cultura de segurança implementada nos últimos 5 anos, responsável por receber mais de 5,5 milhões de visitantes de forma segura.

Normas que seguimos e que regem as inspeções que seguimos 100%.

Decisão Normativa 52, de 25 de agosto de 1994, do CONFEA.

Ato Normativo nº 02, de 14 de dezembro de 2001, CREA-SP.

ABNT NBR 15926:2023, Equipamentos de Parques de Diversão.

ABNT NBR 5410:vigente, Instalações Elétricas de Baixa Tensão.

ABNT NBR 9050, Acessibilidade a Edificações, Mobiliário, Espaços equipamentos urbanos.

ABNT NBR ISO 21101:2014, Turismo de Aventura – Sistema de Gestão de Segurança – Requisitos.

NR 10 - Segurança em Instalações e Serviços em Eletricidade.

NR 13 - Caldeiras, Vasos de Pressão e Tubulações.

Equipe técnica que trabalha dedicada, na atração

1 técnico em mecânica (média de 5h por dia)

1 técnico em elétrica (média de 2h por dia)

Não foram analisadas somente documentação, tivemos inspeções e avaliações técnicas dos engenheiros do CAEx para elaboração dos pareceres.

Preventiva diária (realizada diariamente antes da abertura do parque)

5-6 horas de trabalho realizado por um técnico em mecânica

1-2 horas de trabalho realizado por um técnico em elétrica

3-4 horas de trabalho realizado pela equipe de carpintaria (3-4 pessoas)

Preventiva semanal (realizada toda semana nos dias de parque fechado)

6-7 horas de trabalho realizado por um técnico em mecânica

2-3 horas de trabalho realizado por um técnico em elétrica

14-15 horas de trabalho realizado pela equipe de carpintaria (8-9 pessoas)

Preventiva mensal (realizado durante o mês em que foi gerada, conforme programação)

4-6 horas de trabalho realizado por um técnico em mecânica

Anual (realizada nos trens após 1800-2000 horas de trabalho ou a cada dois anos)

30-50 dias de trabalho realizado pela equipe mecânica (2 mecânicos+1 supervisor)

Sobre o registro de 40 reclamações de visitantes

Em resposta ao questionamento da reportagem, cabe destacar a devida proporcionalidade dos dados: o registro de cerca de 40 reclamações na plataforma Reclame Aqui ao longo dos últimos dois anos refere-se a um universo de aproximadamente 1,2 milhão de visitantes que passaram pela Montezum no mesmo período — o que demonstra um índice estatístico irrisório e abaixo da média mundial, diante do expressivo volume de operações da atração.

Em recente manifestação a respeito do assunto, o Ministério Público deu parecer onde destaca que "o histórico operacional demonstra que eventuais queixas de desconforto muscular constituem episódios isolados, inerentes ao impacto físico esperado em equipamentos de tal natureza, sem qualquer padrão de defeito sistêmico no brinquedo ou falha na prestação do serviço", diz o parecer.

Os casos relatados são encaminhados ao SAV (Serviço de Atendimento ao Visitante) que trata com atenção os relatos de queixas sobre lesões ou desconfortos físicos, passíveis em uma atração amplamente anunciada como radical, mantendo contato com o reclamante para inicialmente ouvir seu relato e seguir se necessário com o acompanhamento."

articles.title: Após bater em poste e capotar, motorista tem pertences levados em São Luís | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista voltava de um show e sofreu ferimento no rosto. Após a colisão, celular e cartões de crédito dele foram levados.
articles.summary: Motorista voltava de um show e sofreu ferimento no rosto. Após a colisão, celular e cartões de crédito dele foram levados.
articles.body:
Um carro ficou destruído após bater na base de um poste, por volta das 3h desta segunda-feira (21), na Avenida dos Holandeses, em São Luís . Com o impacto, uma das rodas se soltou e o veículo capotou, parando cerca de 100 metros depois. O motorista sofreu um ferimento no rosto e está fora de perigo.

O motorista, identificado apenas como Jean, é músico e voltava para casa após um show quando perdeu o controle do veículo.

A batida destruiu a parte dianteira do carro e acionou os airbags. Uma das rodas ficou perto do poste atingido, enquanto o veículo parou mais adiante na avenida.

Após o acidente, pertences do motorista foram saqueados. Segundo informações apuradas pela TV Mirante, o celular e cartões de crédito dele foram levados.

articles.body: MUMBAI: A Saturday night dinner at the Romano restaurant at JW Marriott took an unexpected turn after cardiologist Dr Ashok Seth spotted a baby cockroach on his table and said the sight forced him and his companions to leave without finishing their meal.Seth shared the incident on social media, tagging Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner Tukaram Mundhe and the hotel.Seth said the cockroach, which he jokingly named “Roachie”, was on their table at Romano's, the Italian restaurant at JW Marriott Mumbai Sahar, on Saturday night.“Look who came for dinner unexpectedly. ‘Roachie’ - a baby cockroach was on our table wanting to share our dinner at the Romano restaurant at JW Marriott , Sahar , Mumbai, Saturday night!!!” he wrote in his post.Seth said the diners tried to persuade the insect to leave but it refused to move. Taking a humorous dig at the situation, he added, “Despite our persuasion ‘ Roachie’ refused to leave . Maybe wanted Piazza and not Pasta.”The incident, however, ended up taking away the diners' appetite. “But he really took our appetite away. We left,” Seth wrote.Seth also tagged Mundhe, FSSAI and JW Marriott in his post, adding, “Thankfully we are in Mr Munde’s , territory and he most likely will look into this also.”Marriott Bonvoy Assist responded to Seth's post, saying it took the matter seriously and wanted to look into the incident. “Hello Dr. Ahok, thank you for letting us know. articles.title: Oxford grooming gang survivors tell BBC 'hundreds' of abusers still free
articles.summary: Men who sexually abused them as underage girls are still walking around the city, they say.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual violence

Survivors of an Oxford grooming gang say they still see men who sexually abused them, and who have not been brought to justice, walking around the city.

"A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant - everywhere you can imagine - you'll see a man that's done something," one survivor, Sarah, tells BBC Panorama.

Sarah and two other survivors believe "hundreds" of perpetrators are still free. An ex-police detective who led the initial investigation into grooming gangs in Oxford agrees.

It is the first time that Sarah (whose name we have changed) and one of the other women have spoken out publicly about what they were subjected to.

Gangs of men were found to have sexually exploited and abused underage girls in several towns and cities - including Rotherham, Rochdale and Telford, as well as Oxford - between the 1990s and 2010s.

Oxford was one of the places where most of the perpetrators were identified as older men of Pakistani heritage. In some cases, such as in Rotherham, police were accused of hesitating to act out of fear of being seen as racist. But in Oxford a serious case review found no evidence that this had been a factor.

Now, the government has launched a national inquiry to address why vulnerable children were not protected in England and Wales - including whether attitudes to the girls or the ethnicity of the perpetrators contributed to the failings.

Sarah says she was sexually abused and plied with heroin from the age of 11. More than two decades later, three men were found guilty of abusing her after she testified against them in court. They were jailed for between five and 24 years in 2020.

But it was too little, too late for Sarah, who has battled drug addiction for most her life and has spent time in jail.

"I think they should stay in there forever, because obviously they've taken my life," she says.

Chloe, another survivor whose name we have changed, says she also sees some of her abusers in her local area. Like many survivors, she chose not to go through a police investigation.

"It's difficult because this is where I live, it's where I grew up. There is a few of them that I've seen a few times, even just in the supermarket, driving around," she explains.

She feels "sick, cold" when she sees them, she says.

A third woman, Rachel - again, whose name we have changed - was abused between the ages of 12 to 15 and says many of those men are still free.

She was a key witness in the first trial of Oxford grooming gang members, in 2013, when seven men were convicted.

That trial revealed the grooming, trafficking and rape of six girls over an eight year-period in the city.

But subsequent prosecutions have identified many more victims, and it was estimated in 2015 that more than 370 children were affected.

Rachel says, for years, police did not believe her when she told them what was happening to her. She and the other women say the investigations have not gone far enough.

Thames Valley Police works tirelessly to investigate offenders involved in these horrific crimes and bring them to justice, a spokesperson said.

"It is never too late to come forward", the spokesperson continued, and the force will listen and do everything it can to support victims, survivors and their families.

Trapped in a cycle of abuse and addiction

Sarah says the cigarettes she was given by her groomers were laced with heroin.

"My addiction through my whole life now has resulted from them giving us those cigarettes," she says.

She agreed not to take drugs before speaking to Panorama and received support from her case worker.

Sarah says the men who gave her the cigarettes - and alcohol - then told her she was in debt and needed to have sex with them in order to pay them back.

"They're like, 'well you know, you owe me this money now, so you're going to have to do this'," she says.

"They used to say 'drink this, drink that' to the point where I'm throwing up and sick. Having to be in them houses and feeling trapped. They used to just lock us in.

"Then before you know it, there's one, two, six, seven people turning up. You're just outnumbered, basically."

Rachel, from the age of 12, also found herself in a cycle of sexual abuse and drug addiction. She was trafficked to other towns and cities where men paid the gang for sex with her.

A police officer even tried to take advantage of her in Oxford, she says, but she never reported the incident.

"I was put in the back of a police van on the Cowley Road and there was two male officers and one of them said, 'Well, we know what you're about.'" He then asked her to perform oral sex on him, she says.

Despite a total of 21 men now having been convicted in connection with the Oxford grooming gang, Rachel says there are many perpetrators who have never faced consequences.

"There are a lot of people out there who have been involved in this to some degree or another, that have just been allowed to get on with their lives that were involved in the sexual abuse of children."

As one of the hidden victims of the Oxford grooming gang, none of Chloe's abusers have faced justice for the crimes committed against her.

Until now, she has told just a handful of people about what happened to her from the age of 13. Her account of what happened follows a familiar pattern. The men would befriend her, pay for things, ply her with alcohol, and then tell her she was in debt and sexually abuse her.

"They'd pick us up and there'd be like this random old man in the car and then we'd go to this flat, for example," recalls Chloe, now in her thirties.

Asked what then happened in the flats, she says: "Just the same as always - they'd rape us."

If you have been affected by issues of sexual abuse or violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Former senior detective Simon Morton, who led the initial grooming investigation in Oxford, accepts both he and his force failed at first to understand what was happening.

"It's crazy, it's just ridiculous, the amount of people that were involved," says Morton.

"We should've done more. It's tragic," he says, adding that he believes this type of abuse is "absolutely" still taking place in Oxford.

"We got the core group, that doesn't mean there isn't more.

"I'd like them all convicted, but identification is super hard. The girls were quite often drugged… thrown in a room with a mattress on the floor, and there'd be a procession of men going in all night, all day."

He believed the women's accounts, "but it's another thing trying to take it to court, trying to get a victim a year later to stand up in court, having gone through everything that they go through… to keep opening it up again and again".

The women we spoke to continue to live with the consequences of what happened to them.

"I've not been emotionally there for my kids, because I'm not emotionally there for myself," says Sarah.

Chloe says becoming a mother "made me realise how sick what they did was".

"It really brought it all up again. I really panic about the future and how I can keep her [daughter's] life safe."

For Rachel, any public perception that all the perpetrators have been jailed, and justice has been served, "just isn't reflective of what's really gone on".

"I just want something on this scale to never ever be repeated again," she says.

"It's the biggest scandal in a lifetime."

articles.title: How to prepare yourself for when an emergency strikes
articles.summary: BBC South speaks to experts and residents about how they would plan for a national emergency.
articles.body:
How would you prepare for an emergency? How would you cope? And what about your relatives, friends, neighbours and colleagues?

These are the questions the government wants people to ask themselves, as emergency planners warn of growing threats from heatwaves and flooding, as well as potential cyber attacks by hostile states that could cripple vital energy infrastructure.

This summer's wildfires, which scorched fields in areas including Swallowfield in Berkshire, Abingdon in Oxfordshire, and forced the closure of the A31 in the New Forest, have highlighted just how vulnerable communities can be to natural disasters.

The government says there are a number of simple but effective steps everyone can take to stay safe and better prepared should disaster strike.

Back in August, the threat of wildfires saw the government send out emergency text alerts to people's mobiles.

The siren-like alarm was so unexpected it interrupted live TV programmes and theatre shows, catching millions off guard.

While that was a deliberately dramatic move to catch attention, the government's website advises people to keep a list of items at home in case of an emergency.

It suggests you have the following close at hand:

Portable power bank for your mobile phone

Battery or wind-up radio to get updates during a power cut

Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for hygiene purposes when the water is off

Bottled water – there is no standard figure as emergencies can vary in duration

Non-perishable food such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables plus tin opener

Prof Hannah Cloke is a climate scientist at the University of Reading and an expert in risk and resilience.

She says the idea of having enough supplies ready to keep you going for two to three days makes perfect sense.

"It is a little bit scary for some people I think, but what we really need to think about is how we can prepare better because, in preparing better, it actually becomes less scary," she says.

It is easy to think "yes I get it - but it'll never really happen to me, why bother?"

In Lisbon on business and 1,200 miles away from his wife back home in the Hampshire village of Broughton, Ricardo Evangelista thought that too.

Until that is Portugal and Spain's electricity networks collapsed.

He remembers the events of 28 April 2026 with near perfect clarity.

"Mobile phone signals and data stopped after about an hour and the office buildings' emergency generators also stopped after an hour," he says.

"Then the ATMs stopped working. Supermarkets closed down and public transport stopped working too."

Power was not fully restored for nearly 24 hours. It was the biggest blackout to hit Europe in 20 years.

Dealing with the practicalities of living in a world without electricity was one thing though.

It is a story Ricardo tells about a colleague that stands out, 18 months on from the blackout.

"We had some colleagues in the office who we sent home," he says.

"One of our colleagues lived with her parents. She left to try and make her way home. Two hours later, her father showed up in the office. When he told him that she left two hours ago he looked so worried."

Father and daughter were later reunited and all ended well - but that story and Ricardo's memory of the day the lights went out points to an uncomfortable truth.

Our society is gobbling up energy at a rate of knots.

Cyber security experts say the rapid growth of AI and the data centres that go alongside them in places like Slough and Portsmouth means our energy network is becoming increasingly vulnerable to attack from hostile states.

It is a threat our policy makers are well aware of and another reason why they want us to be able to look after ourselves if our critical infrastructure is targeted.

Rafael Narezzi is the chief executive officer of the cyber security firm Centrii.

He says: "The digital economy that we have today isn't ready for what's happening with the geo-political.

"Today, energy is more critical than ever. We have technology companies across the country but we haven't done the work to keep them safe and secure."

The government is getting ready to launch a public awareness campaign later this year to help people prepare for emergencies.

Cabinet Office Minister Darren Jones also says it will carry out the "largest UK home defence exercise in several decades" next year to ensure the UK is ready "should the worst ever happen".

Ricardo says his experience of the day the lights went out in Lisbon shows two things.

One, how reliant we have become on electricity to carry out even the most basic tasks and how quickly things can take a turn for the worst

Two, how important it is to be ready just in case calamity strikes.

He now has batteries, torches and phone chargers dotted around his house in Hampshire, saying, almost bashfully, he is now the proud owner of several wind up radios.

No doubt the government would be proud of him too.

articles.title: Quadruple amputee from Oxford enters the Big Brother house
articles.summary: Charlotte lost her arms and legs to meningitis as a toddler and is now a contestant on Big Brother.
articles.body:
Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back.

The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was just two years old.

Now 18, Charlotte is a contestant in the latest series of Big Brother, something she has dreamed about for most of her life.

Her dad, Alex, told BBC Radio Oxford he was anxious about her appearance on the show, but said there had never been much point telling his daughter not to do something she had her sights on.

That resilience was on full display within seconds of Charlotte's arrival on the show.

During the launch, her shoe broke as she stepped out to be introduced, and she had to remove her prosthetic legs on stage before entering the house.

"Maybe it was my fate to walk in with no legs," she told the diary room. "Maybe that was just what was meant to happen."

She added that she was used to going without her prosthetics at home.

"When I'm at home, I have my legs off all the time," she said. "When I'm cooking, I have my legs off. I like to be four foot. I like to be tiny, like a little tiny doll."

Alex said the moment had summed up his daughter's unstoppable nature perfectly.

Charlotte applied for the show earlier this year - the first time she had been old enough to enter - and made it through a process her dad said involved around 50,000 applicants.

"She's wanted to go in there since she was about five or six," he said. "I think she used to watch it religiously with her mum."

Charlotte had applied without telling her dad and had already completed several interviews with producers before he found out.

He admitted he had struggled to come to terms with her decision to apply.

"I thought she was on a wind-up to start with," he said. "She was dead serious. I've been in bits for about three months."

But Alex said there was little point trying to stand in her way.

"You try telling someone like Charlotte that she's not allowed to do something," he said.

"We've gone her whole life trying to tell her that she can't do stuff, and she's just taken on that mantle."

Since she turned 16, he said she had taken charge of every decision relating to her own care and prosthetics.

Alex said his daughter had the resilience to handle whatever reaction she received from the public.

"Every day is a struggle for her, more than for anybody else," he said. "But she's got skin as thick as a rhino's. I take my hat off to her."

Charlotte said she expected viewers watching her around the clock to be surprised by how ordinary her daily life actually was.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

"People are surprised at anything I do, even normal things like cooking, doing my makeup, getting dressed," she said. "They're probably going to be surprised at the most normal things for me."

Asked what she would do with the prize money if she won, Charlotte said her prosthetic legs cost around £25,000 each.

"I probably would put a lot of it into savings," she said. "My prosthetic legs are about £25,000 per leg, so probably put half in savings and then the other half... just go on a nice holiday, just kind of spend it."

Caroline Hughes, senior support services Manager for Meningitis Research Foundation, said the long term consequences of the disease "remain widely misunderstood".

"Every day, we support people navigating the physical, emotional and practical challenges that can follow a meningitis diagnosis," she said.

"That's why it is so powerful to see people like Charlotte sharing their experience on a platform like Big Brother.

"By speaking so openly about her story, she is helping bring greater understanding of the long-term impact meningitis can have, while also enabling others affected by the disease to feel seen, heard and less alone."

The 23rd series of Big Brother began on 13 September and will last 54 days, making it the longest series since 2017.

ITV said the series had been "reimagined as a house of surprises" and viewers could expect "ambitious tasks, high-stakes nominations and dramatic live evictions".

articles.title: Calls for Jèrriais and English on Jersey street signs
articles.summary: A lawyer thinks putting Jèrriais on Jersey street signs could foster island pride.
articles.body:
There are calls to put Jèrriais on Jersey street signs to familiarise people with the native language and foster a sense of island pride.

Carl Parslow, partner at Parslow's law firm, said he wanted politicians to adopt the Welsh model where public signage must be in both English and Welsh, and place Jèrriais alongside English.

In 2019, the States Assembly agreed that Jèrriais should be incorporated into official States signs. However, the language is absent on the new government building.

A government spokesperson said a new Jèrriais strategy was being developed and signage at the Union Street building would be updated.

While Jèrriais was the mother-tongue for most people born in Jersey as late as the 1930s, its decline was dramatically accelerated by the German Occupation during World War Two and now its estimated that about 200 people speak it.

Parslow said the aim of his idea was not to make everyone speak it again, but to get more people familiar with words from the island's historic language.

"Languages survive through visibility. Most people in Wales are not fluent Welsh speakers, but they encounter the language every day," he said.

"Seeing it regularly gives it relevance and helps ensure its survival."

Prof Martin Shipman, associate editor for Welsh news service Nation.Cymru, said it had been a success.

"It familiarises and normalises the language so people accept it. Surveys have shown that most people appreciate hearing Welsh even if they don't understand it," he said.

Shipman said it had also had a cultural impact and "helped people regain and sense of their own identity".

Tama Coxshall, a 19-year-old Jèrriais content creator, sad he thought displaying the language would develop the island's national pride.

He said: "Jersey people will so frequently relate to the UK and have that as our cultural reference when Jersey is just as important.

"Having billingual signs and Jèrriais in products in shops... gives people licence to feel they can be proud of being from Jersey."

The influencer said he would also like to see the government place the language on States signs, as was agreed in 2019, with the "government committing to the policy and the promises it's made to the Jersey people, which is all of us".

A government spokesperson said: "Signage at the government building on Union Street is currently being updated as part of wider improvements reflecting our commitment to promoting Jèrriais as an important part of Jersey's cultural identity.

"A new Jèrriais strategy is being developed to improve its visibility in areas such as signage, and a Jerriais Advisory Group is being re-established later this year."

articles.title: An Austrian family bakery opened a New York shop selling a 3.3-pound rye loaf for $60; the bread uses organic rye flour, water and salt, ferments for up to 24 hours and is the store's only loaf
articles.summary: In a city where a bagel can be breakfast, lunch and a minor cultural institution, one new bakery is asking New Yorkers to rethink what bread can cost..
articles.body: In a city where a bagel can be breakfast, lunch and a minor cultural institution, one new bakery is asking New Yorkers to rethink what bread can cost. In the heart of Soho, an Austrian family business has opened a shop devoted to just one loaf: a roughly 3.3-pound rye sourdough priced at $60, informs Euro News. But the question is what makes it so unique and pricey? As per the report, there are no shelves crowded with croissants, pastries or a dozen different breads. Instead, the bakery centers its operation around a single traditional rye loaf, made with organic rye flour, water and salt and fermented naturally. Scroll down to read the details.A bakery built around one loafThe new shop, called Rye, is located on Lafayette Street and brings the baking traditions of Graz to Manhattan. It is operated by the Auer family, which has built a bakery business with more than 40 locations in Austria, states the Euro News report. The flagship loaf weighs about 1.5 kilograms, or 3.3 pounds, and is made without commercial yeast. Its dough relies on natural sourdough fermentation, with the process taking up to 24 hours.If we go by the news report, the bread is baked in a two-tonne oven imported from Germany, adding another distinctly European element to the Soho operation. The report also states that customers who do not want to commit to an entire $60 loaf can buy smaller portions or slices topped with ingredients such as butter, chocolate spread or caviar.Also, for the unversed, rye gives bread a deeper, earthy, slightly tangy and nutty taste compared with wheat. It has less gluten-forming potential than wheat, so rye breads tend to be denser and chewier rather than light and airy. Also, rye flour is particularly active in fermentation, making it well suited to naturally leavened breads.A recipe with roots in AustriaAccording to the report, rye was chosen as the bakery's sole bread partly because of its importance in Austrian baking. The grain has long played a central role in the country's bread culture, and the Auer family's recipe is said to have been passed down through generations. The method reportedly traces back to a farmer on an Alpine pasture who taught the technique to an older generation of the Auer family. It was later brought back to Graz and developed into the loaf now being sold in New York, states the online report.The bakery's approach also puts fermentation at the center of the product. Unlike bread made with commercial yeast and designed for rapid production, sourdough requires significantly more time, space and labor. That lengthy process contributes to the loaf's dense texture, pronounced flavor and extended freshness while also adding to its production costs.The matter of $60There is little mystery about why the price has attracted attention. At roughly $40 per kilogram, the Soho loaf sits far above ordinary bread prices in both New York and Europe. Traditional sourdough in New York can already command $10 to $20 per loaf, while specialty bakeries regularly charge more for labor-intensive products. Even so, $60 places Rye in an entirely different category, explains the news report. The price reflects more than ingredients. The bakery operates in one of Manhattan's most expensive neighborhoods, while its production involves imported equipment, specialty ingredients and a slow fermentation process.Luxury bread finds its audienceTo date, critics have questioned whether bread should become a luxury product, particularly when the basic ingredients are so simple. Others see the loaf differently, pointing to the quality of the ingredients, the traditional recipe and the labor involved in producing a naturally fermented bread. In Soho, where premium food experiences are hardly unusual, Rye appears to be betting that there is an audience willing to pay for exactly that.Image Courtesy: istockLooking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Denver's historic bank building was bought for $17.6 million and got a $22.4 million renovation; after WeWork left, the 107,630-sq-ft property is now 100% vacant
articles.summary: US News: Denver’s historic bank building at 821 17th Street remains completely vacant despite a $22.4 million renovation after its owner bought the property fo.
articles.body: Denver’s historic bank building at 821 17th Street remains completely vacant despite a $22.4 million renovation after its owner bought the property for $17.6 million in 2017. The nine-storey building, now known as The Vault, has 107,630 square feet of office and retail space in the heart of downtown Denver’s former financial district.According to The Denver Gazette, the building was originally constructed in 1907 and was later redesigned by architects Fisher & Fisher. It was designated a Denver Landmark in 1977. The property was one of the financial buildings that once formed the 'Wall Street of the Rockies', when the area around 17th, Champa and Stout streets was a major centre of Denver’s commercial activity.Harbor Associates, based in Seal Beach, California, bought the building in 2017. The owner later invested more than $22.4 million in improvements, including a new lobby, restoration of the first and second floors, exterior facade work and upgrades to the building’s mechanical systems. JLL is now presenting the property for sale as an opportunity for office use, adaptive reuse or conversion into residential or hospitality space.Finding tenants has proved difficult, however. WeWork leased about 40,000 square feet of the building in 2018 but left in 2021 as the pandemic changed office-working patterns.A historic building The Vault’s current situation reflects a much wider change in Upper Downtown Denver. Office vacancies across downtown have remained high, although they have dipped slightly to around 38%, according to The Denver Gazette. Some newer office properties have also been sold at heavily reduced prices, with buyers considering residential conversions as one possible way to reuse the space.The area around The Vault once went through another major transformation. Downtown Denver’s historic commercial districts had struggled during the 1960s, when older buildings deteriorated and businesses moved away. By the 1980s and 1990s, however, parts of downtown were becoming active again as Denver developed into a sports and entertainment centre.The former bank building itself became part of that revival. Its large basement vault became the centrepiece of the Broker Restaurant, which opened in 1972 and remained there until it closed permanently in 2017. In 1978, the building also became home to Women’s Bank, which was widely recognised for its focus on women-owned businesses and lending to women.The $22.4 million renovationJLL’s property listing describes The Vault as a 'fully repositioned' 107,630-square-foot office and retail landmark. It says eight of the building’s nine floors have been renovated and are ready for occupation, with furnished office suites.The listing says the property is being offered without existing leases. That gives a potential buyer the option to continue with office use or use it for residential or hospitality conversion.The building also has a two-storey entrance with a 23-foot ceiling. JLL describes the atrium as a major feature of the property. The listing also highlights restored historic details, including stained-glass skylights, hand-painted ceiling beams and a sculpted mezzanine frieze.However, The Denver Gazette also reported that a view through the locked doors of the main floor showed areas that appeared to need additional finish work.Could the bank become homes?The possibility of converting The Vault into residential space is being considered as downtown Denver looks for ways to reduce its large amount of unused office space.Bill Mosher, a former chief project officer for the Denver Downtown Development Authority, said historic buildings can have advantages when they are converted.“Generally, historic buildings have real possibilities,” Mosher told The Denver Gazette. “They have lobbies that are interesting spaces.”The Vault has an L-shaped design, with the two wings measuring about 50 feet wide. That layout could provide window access and floor plans that may work for apartments, according to the report. The building is also much smaller in scale than some newer downtown office towers.However, architect-engineer Bradley L. Zieg said converting an office building into homes is not simple because the two types of buildings are designed differently.“Most buildings of any kind of stature were designed and built to a specific use,” Zieg told The Denver Gazette. “Converting offices into residential uses is a real stretch. Residential architecture is fundamentally different than whatever else you would do,” he said.Zieg also pointed to problems involving heating, cooling, ventilation and plumbing. “Even if you can solve the space-planning problem, now you’ve got all the plumbing. You’ve got all the provided heat and cooling. It’s a nightmare.”Newer buildings sold at steep discountsThe challenge for The Vault is that some newer downtown properties have changed hands at much lower prices. Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Asher Luzzatto has bought four buildings covering a combined 1.75 million square feet.Those purchases included the Denver Energy Center, which was reportedly bought for $5.25 million after having sold for $176 million a decade earlier.Mosher said the low purchase prices make such conversions easier to consider. “The reason Luzzatto is doing those is that he bought them for less than 10 bucks a foot,” Mosher said. “It’s hard to do that with $29 million sunk into building.”Downtown's vacancy challengeGreg Paugh, vice president and broker at Stream Realty Partners, said The Vault reflects the wider uncertainty facing downtown Denver.“For several institutional owners that have been trying to hold strong, they’ve decided it’s time to cut bait and for the few playing the long game, betting on Denver’s recovery, it’s another opportunity to capitalise on another heavily discounted sale,” Paugh said.Paugh said demand may be shifting from LoDo towards areas farther east of Larimer Street. He also said some tenants were moving from Cherry Creek and the Denver Tech Center.“The Vault sits firmly in the CBD, and this may help downtown’s perception if it truly can be revitalised,” Paugh said.He added that he did not expect the historic building to sell at the single-digit prices seen for some newer towers. But he said “it will not be in the first wave of downtown comebacks.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Days before Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march, former prime minister Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed.In a series of posts on X, Kasim alleged that his aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with cousins Shershah and Shahrez, were taken from their homes after authorities allegedly entered the properties and forced them into vehicles. The claims could not be independently verified.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noureen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez have now been abducted as well,” Kasim said.“They have broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. He subsequently said the children were safe but alleged that two more cousins, Azeem and Sakeenah, had also been taken into custody.“Hearing news that my cousin’s children are now safe. Meanwhile, two more of my cousins have been arrested. Azeem and Sakeenah. No reasons given. No location given,” he said.The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan in Lahore on Sunday. She was ordered to be held for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, with the authorities citing public safety and order concerns. She was later taken to Kot Lakhpat jail, according to police and Pakistani media reports.Aleema's detention ahead of PTI marchLahore deputy commissioner Muhammad Ali Ijaz issued the detention order under the MPO law. The order cited allegations involving protests, roadblocks and the mobilisation of PTI workers.PTI chairman barrister Gohar Ali Khan condemned Aleema's detention and demanded her release, arguing that it could further increase tensions ahead of the September 27 demonstration.Aleema's son Shahrez had earlier alleged that his mother was “abducted” after leaving her home and said the family had no information about where she had been taken.The PTI march is being organised to demand the release of Imran Khan, who remains in jail and is facing multiple legal cases. articles.title: Australia ageing population crisis report sparks migration debate
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For the first time in the 2060s, deaths are projected to outnumber births in Australia, while annual population growth is expected to average 0.9% ove.
articles.body: For the first time in the 2060s, deaths are projected to outnumber births in Australia, while annual population growth is expected to average 0.9% over the next four decades. Lower fertility and declining net overseas migration are expected to contribute to the slowdown, according to the Australian Treasury's 2026 Intergenerational Report released on Monday.That compares with average population growth of 1.4% a year over the previous four decades. Net overseas migration — migrant arrivals minus departures — is projected to decline further before levelling off.Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the number of Australians aged over 85 would triple by 2066, increasing demand for health services.Labor introduced tighter immigration rules last week amid rising support for One Nation, which has called for steep reductions in immigration. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's approval rating also fell to its lowest level since he took office in 2022, Reuters reported.For decades, migrant inflows have supported Australia's population growth despite persistently low birth rates. Japan, Germany and South Korea already record more deaths than births; Australia is projected to reach that point in the 2060s.Treasury's 40-year outlook is built around five major shifts: the artificial intelligence revolution, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, aging and the care economy, and Australia's industrial transformation.Future budgets could include further tax cuts. The government has also been providing cost-of-living support as households contend with elevated inflation, mortgage costs and expensive housing.Older regions could face care-sector labour shortagesAn older population is expected to require more care services. Staffing pressures are projected to be greater in regions with older populations, particularly in healthcare and aged care, where migrant workers form an important part of the workforce.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Usher first saw L.A. Reid’s Alpharetta mansion at 13 and dreamed of owning it; at 21 he paid $1.2 million, modernised the 10,823-sq-ft home and sold it for $1.5 million nearly two decades later
articles.summary: US News: Some childhood dreams stay fantasies; Usher turned one into reality. At 13, Usher had already formed a connection with a mansion he would eventually c.
articles.body: Some childhood dreams stay fantasies; Usher turned one into reality. At 13, Usher had already formed a connection with a mansion he would eventually call his own. In 1991, the future R&B superstar visited music producer L.A. Reid’s home in Alpharetta, Georgia, and was captivated by the property. Years later, Usher recalled on BET’s show How I’m Living that he walked through the house and thought he wanted to own it one day. Eight years later, at just 21, he turned that childhood ambition into reality, purchasing Reid’s former residence for $1.2 million.The mansion that caught Usher’s eye at 13When Usher first visited the Alpharetta property in 1991, L.A. Reid, the influential music producer and co-founder of LaFace Records, owned it. Reid had converted one of the rooms into a recording studio for his label, giving the house an especially strong connection to the music industry. Years later, Usher recalled the visit on a 2003 episode of BET’s How I’m Living, describing how mesmerised he was by the house and how he remembered wanting to own it someday.By the time Usher was 21, his career was already gaining momentum. His music was attracting major attention, he had appeared on the television sitcom Moesha and completed his first film, The Faculty. That was also when the opportunity to buy the house he had admired as a teenager finally arrived.Usher paid $1.2 million for the home at 21In 1999, Usher purchased the Alpharetta mansion for $1.2 million. The 10,823-square-foot residence offered the scale and elaborate interiors associated with a high-end celebrity home of the era. Architectural Digest describes a grand foyer featuring black marble columns, while an open hallway on the second floor overlooked the living room. The living space had a black marble fireplace framed by built-in mahogany bookcases. The primary bedroom also featured a distinctive black-and-gold poster bed. The home’s design was dramatic, with dark finishes and ornate details throughout. Its large size also gave the young musician plenty of room to create spaces suited to both entertaining and his career.For Usher, however, the significance of the purchase went beyond the property itself. He was buying a home he had first seen eight years earlier, when he was still a teenager imagining what his future might look like.He modernised the mansion in his own styleThe house already had a distinctive appearance when Usher bought it, but he later made a series of changes to give the interiors a more contemporary and personal feel. According to Realtor.com, he replaced the original wrought-iron and glass front door with a wooden one. The wrought-iron and mahogany staircase railing was also replaced with muted grey wood.The living room underwent a notable transformation. The original built-in bookcases were replaced with floating shelves, while the fireplace received a wooden mantel and herringbone-patterned brick, giving the space a more rustic appearance. The kitchen was similarly updated. Its central island was transformed into a muted teal design topped with marble. A farmhouse sink, sliding metal door, bench seating and rustic tables added a more relaxed look to the space. The bathrooms were also redesigned with vintage-style tile, white marble and glass shower doors.A home shaped around Usher’s careerSome of the mansion’s most distinctive spaces reflected Usher’s life as a performer. The property included a dedicated dance studio equipped with floor-to-ceiling mirrors and a substantial sound system. That was alongside a home theatre, yoga studio, spa and sauna. Outside, the property offered a heated pool and summer kitchen, adding to its entertainment-focused layout.Nearly two decades later, Usher sold the mansionUsher remained the owner of the Alpharetta property for nearly two decades. During those years, his career expanded dramatically, transforming him from a young performer into one of the most recognised names in R&B and pop music. In 2018, the mansion finally went on the market. Realtor.com and Architectural Digest reported that Usher sold the property for $1.5 million in June of that year.The transaction brought an end to an unusual real-estate story that had begun with a 13-year-old visiting a music producer’s home. Eight years after that first visit, Usher had purchased the same property for $1.2 million. He then spent years updating the 10,823-square-foot mansion to reflect his own tastes and lifestyle before eventually selling it for $1.5 million. What makes the Alpharetta house particularly notable is not simply its size, celebrity ownership or amenities. It was a property Usher had wanted since he was a teenager, making its eventual purchase at 21 a rare example of a childhood real-estate dream becoming reality.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Gary Anderson: Confidence 'damaged' by on-the-run killer case - Long
articles.summary: Gary Anderson remains at large a week after he absconded while attending his father's funeral in Derry.
articles.body:
Public confidence in the justice system has been "damaged" by the circumstances surrounding the temporary release from prison of convicted murderer Gary Anderson, Justice Minister Naomi Long has said.

Anderson, who is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the 2018 murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry, remains at large a week after he absconded while attending his father's funeral in Londonderry last Monday.

Long, who is to meet the murder victim's family, is ordering an independent review into the circumstances surrounding Anderson's release from Maghaberry Prison.

That happened after a court overturned a decision by the prison service to refuse him permission to attend the funeral.

A day before the funeral last Monday, a judge granted Anderson a two-hour compassionate temporary release (CTR) from Maghaberry Prison to attend.

Anderson's brother Sean also challenged the decision not to release him from Magilligan Prison to attend the funeral, but that was upheld by the same judge.

The funeral service took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry last Monday morning.

Anderson was not given permission to attend cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, in the Republic of Ireland that afternoon.

At some stage on Monday morning, he absconded from his court-approved civilian chaperone.

CTR can be granted to prisoners when a family member has died or is seriously ill, but the decision to release them takes into account the circumstances of the case and any risks involved.

Questions have been raised over the granting of Anderson's CTR following the publication of the full 15-page judgement from the judicial review into the Prison Service's decision.

Why was Anderson granted compassionate temporary release?

The judgement found that the decision to refuse Anderson's request was based on inaccurate information about the risk he posed.

The decision had been taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison.

In his judgement, Mr Justice Rooney found that an internal assessment of Anderson's likelihood of reoffending had been recorded at a higher level than the score held on the Prison Service's internal system.

A legal representative for the Prison Service told the court that the increased score had come from a colleague rather than the duty governor's personal knowledge.

When the system was checked, Anderson's score was 27, indicating a medium likelihood of reoffending, rather than 32, which had been recorded as a high likelihood in the decision letter.

The judge found that the duty governor "clearly took account of this incorrect information" when assessing the risks and considering whether the decision was proportionate.

There is a question mark about what happened after the judge knocked back the original decision.

According to the judgement, the judge invited the duty governor to reconsider the decision, but that offer was declined.

The judge described the decision not to review it as "somewhat surprising" and he granted Anderson temporary release subject to a number of conditions, finding that the Prison Service's decision was "flawed" and had taken into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors".

The judge said the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment was unlawful.

However Long, whose department oversees the Prison Service, has said a procedural failing by the Departmental Solicitor's Office (DSO), meant prison officials were not told that the judge had offered them the chance to reconsider their decision not to release Anderson.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Monday, Long said: "We have identified that that offer was not passed onto the decision-makers within Prison Service at that time and so we have only become aware of it when the full judgement was actually published and we were then able to refer to the transcripts."

She said she was setting up an independent review into what had happened as the offer was not made to the Prison Service so the judge "in good faith made the decision based on the information that he had".

Long has said all relevant facts must be established and carefully considered and is to update MLAs on Monday about the case.

She said she was convinced of the need for an independent review because public confidence in the system had been damaged.

"I want to be absolutely confident that we have all of the facts of the case and that we can take mitigating measures to ensure that there is no repetition of this."

Speaking on Monday, Long apologised to the family of Karol Kelly and acknowledged the impact Anderson's release and subsequent absconding from prison has had.

She said she was "desperately sorry that they have been put through this trauma as a result of whatever has happened".

"Whatever miscommunication, whatever poor information, they should not have been subjected to this ongoing trauma and distress, and I can only apologise genuinely for that."

She said she would meet them "subject to their wishes" and added: "I don't want them to be drawn into this, I don't want them to feel any further distress."

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said the "ongoing drip-feed of information" surrounding the case was "shattering confidence in the justice system and the justice minister".

Speaking at Stormont, he claimed the Northern Ireland Assembly was "misled" when questions were raised last week about how Anderson became unlawfully at large.

"Whether that was inadvertent or because the right questions just simply hadn't been asked, it's not good enough," he said.

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said Karol Kelly's family had been "retraumatised by the catastrophic failures".

Burrows said he was "not impressed" by how Long had handled the controversy, saying that when he "raised these issues in the assembly last week" she "brushed them off".

Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson said Long "did not at any point mislead the assembly" and commended her "openness" and "transparency".

"The minister put on the record the information that was provided to her, and as soon as concerns arose around that information the minister wrote to the speaker to ask to go to the chamber to provide additional information," he said.

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna described the case as a "very serious situation".

The MP, whose party forms the official opposition at Stormont, said their assembly members would be "seeking to hold the justice minister to account".

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said the situation was "beyond comprehension".

He said there were "many serious questions" for the Prison Service and Stormont's departmental solicitors' office, as well as the judiciary.
